cards.prompt: Create a Series of 3 prices with custom labels 'a', 'b', 'c' instead of the default integer index.
cards.why: The index argument lets you label each value with anything meaningful — not just 0, 1, 2 — right from creation.
cards.whenToUse: The values naturally have a label (a date, an id, a name) rather than a plain position.
cards.commonMistake: Passing an index list of the wrong length — pandas raises a ValueError instead of padding or truncating.

cards.prompt: Get the name of the revenue column, treated as a Series.
cards.why: Every Series carries a name, which is exactly the column name when it came from a DataFrame — it travels with the values.
cards.whenToUse: Building generic code that needs to know a Series' label without hardcoding it.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting a standalone Series (not pulled from a DataFrame) has name=None until you set one.

cards.prompt: Rename the revenue Series to 'sales' without touching the original df.
cards.why: rename() on a Series returns a new Series with a different name — it doesn't rename the column in the source DataFrame.
cards.whenToUse: Giving a Series a clearer label before combining it with others, e.g. before pd.concat.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting df's column to be renamed too — for that you'd use df.rename(columns=...) on the DataFrame itself.

cards.prompt: Convert the revenue Series into a plain Python list.
cards.why: tolist() strips away the index and dtype, leaving a plain list of native Python values.
cards.whenToUse: Passing values to code that expects a plain list, not a pandas object.
cards.commonMistake: Using list(df['revenue']) instead — it works too, but tolist() also converts numpy scalar types (like numpy.int64) to native Python types, which list() alone doesn't.

cards.prompt: Get the distinct values in the region column, in order of first appearance.
cards.why: unique() returns a NumPy array of distinct values, preserving first-seen order rather than sorting them.
cards.whenToUse: Checking what categories actually appear in a column before grouping or filtering by them.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting sorted output — unique() does not sort; use sorted(df['region'].unique()) if you need that.

cards.prompt: Count how many distinct regions appear in df.
cards.why: nunique() is shorthand for len(df['region'].unique()) — a direct count instead of building the array first.
cards.whenToUse: You need the count of distinct values, not the values themselves.
cards.commonMistake: Calling len() on the Series itself — that counts all rows, not distinct values.

cards.prompt: Count how many rows fall into each region.
cards.why: value_counts() returns a Series of counts per distinct value, sorted from most to least common by default.
cards.whenToUse: Getting a frequency breakdown of a categorical column at a glance.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting the result in the order values first appear — it's sorted by count (descending), not by appearance.
cards.example:
# West     3
# East     3
# North    2
# Name: count, dtype: int64

cards.prompt: Convert the revenue Series (currently int64) to float.
cards.why: astype() changes a Series' dtype explicitly, returning a new Series rather than modifying in place.
cards.whenToUse: A column loaded with the wrong type (e.g. numbers stored as text) needs converting before arithmetic works correctly.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting astype() doesn't modify df in place — you need to reassign, e.g. df['revenue'] = df['revenue'].astype(float).

cards.prompt: Replace each category value using a lookup dict: Shoes -> Footwear, Bags -> Accessories.
cards.why: map() applies a dict (or function) element-wise to a Series — values not found in the dict become NaN.
cards.whenToUse: Recoding a categorical column using a known, fixed lookup table.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming unmapped values are left unchanged — map() replaces anything missing from the dict with NaN, not the original value.

cards.prompt: Apply a 10% markup to every value in the revenue Series using a lambda.
cards.why: apply() runs a function against every element — useful for logic too custom for a built-in vectorized method.
cards.whenToUse: The transformation isn't a simple arithmetic op or a fixed lookup (that's what map()/vectorized ops are for).
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for apply() when plain vectorized arithmetic (df['revenue'] * 1.1) would do the same thing faster.

cards.prompt: Subtract the units Series from the revenue Series, element by element.
cards.why: Arithmetic between two Series aligns by index first, then operates element-wise — not just by position.
cards.whenToUse: Computing a new value from two existing columns, e.g. a difference or a ratio.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming this works purely by position — if the two Series have different indexes, pandas aligns by label and introduces NaN for anything that doesn't match.

cards.prompt: Add up every value in the revenue Series into a single total.
cards.why: sum() reduces a Series to one scalar — the total across every row.
cards.whenToUse: A single overall total is needed, rather than a per-group breakdown (that's groupby's job).
cards.commonMistake: Calling sum() on the whole DataFrame (df.sum()) when you only meant one column — that sums every numeric column separately.

cards.prompt: Get the index label of the row with the highest revenue.
cards.why: idxmax() returns the label where the maximum occurs, not the maximum value itself — max() would give you the value.
cards.whenToUse: You need to know which row is the maximum, e.g. to look up its other columns afterward.
cards.commonMistake: Confusing idxmax() (returns a label) with argmax() (returns an integer position) — they usually agree with a default RangeIndex, but diverge once the index isn't 0..n.

cards.prompt: Get the first value of the revenue Series by position, regardless of what its index label happens to be. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: iloc works on a Series the same way it does on a DataFrame — strictly by integer position, ignoring labels.
cards.whenToUse: The Series might have a non-default index (e.g. after a filter or sort), but you still want 'the first row' by position.
cards.commonMistake: Using df['revenue'][0] instead — that looks up label 0, which raises a KeyError if row 0 was previously dropped or sorted away.

cards.prompt: Which correctly marks each row True where revenue is above the average revenue?
cards.why: Comparing a Series to a scalar (here, its own mean) broadcasts the comparison across every element, producing a boolean Series.
cards.whenToUse: Flagging above/below-average rows before filtering or counting them.
cards.commonMistake: Reversing the comparison direction (mean() > df['revenue']) — that flags below-average rows instead, the opposite of what was asked.
cards.example:
# 0     True
# 1     True
# 2     True
# 3    False
# dtype: bool
